introduction: Today the whole Church rejoices with all the saints: not only those whose names we know, but the great multitude, from every nation and language, that no one can count. They were people like us, who let God's love transform them. The Beatitudes are their portrait, and our calling too, for, as John tells us, we are already God's children. As we celebrate, let us ask the saints to pray for us, and tomorrow let us remember all the faithful departed.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us pray with confidence to the Father of all holiness.
intentions: For the Church on earth: that, encouraged by the example and prayers of the saints, all her members may answer the call to holiness. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the peacemakers, the merciful, and all who suffer for what is right: that they may know that God is with them and that their reward is great. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who mourn: that they may be comforted, and that the hope of the resurrection may sustain them. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the young people of our parish: that they may discover in the saints friends and models for their own lives. Let us pray to the Lord.
For all our beloved dead, whom we remember tomorrow: that, washed in the blood of the Lamb, they may join the multitude who praise God forever. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Almighty God, you have given us the joy of honouring all the saints in one celebration. Hear our prayers, and bring us to share their glory. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: A crowd no one can count
reflection.body:
When John is given a glimpse of heaven, he first hears a number: one hundred and forty-four thousand, twelve thousand from each tribe of Israel. It is a number of completeness, the whole people of God. Then he looks, and sees something greater: "a great multitude which no man could count, out of every nation and of all tribes, peoples, and languages," clothed in white and holding palms of victory.

That is today's feast. Some saints we celebrate by name, with their own day in the calendar, but most are unknown to us: mothers and fathers, teachers, labourers, the sick who offered their suffering, ordinary believers who loved God and their neighbour to the end. Many of us can think of someone, a grandparent perhaps, whom we quietly believe to be among them.

Who are these people in white? The elder answers: they have come out of the great tribulation and washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb. Holiness is not first our achievement. It is Christ's gift, received and allowed to change us, often through suffering.

The Beatitudes describe what that change looks like. Jesus calls blessed the poor in spirit, the mourners, the meek, those who hunger for justice, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers and the persecuted. They are not rules so much as a portrait, and the face in it is Christ's own. The saints are those in whom that face became visible.

The Second Vatican Council insisted that all the faithful, in every state of life, are called to the fullness of Christian life and the perfection of charity. Holiness is not for a few specialists. John says it plainly: "now we are children of God," and what we will be has not yet been revealed. The saints show us that it can be done, and they pray for us while we try.

Tomorrow, on All Souls' Day, we pray for those still being purified. Today we lift up our eyes and remember where we are going.
